newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia buries blast victims, vows to find bombers.
newsitem.headline: Russia buries blast victims, vows to find bombers.

text.p: Russia on Thursday buried victims of a weekend bomb blast that killed 14 mourners at a Moscow cemetery, and authorities vowed to track down the killers.
Investigators have linked Sunday's bombing to a longstanding feud between two rival branches of a charity set up to help disabled victims of the Afghan war.
The interior ministry, under fire for failing to combat violent crime, pledged an allout effort to root out the bombers.
Contract killings of bankers, businessmen and even members of national and local parliaments are nearly an everyday affair in post-communist Russia. Most of them remain unsolved.
Fearing further attacks, police mounted a tight security operation around the church in central Moscow where a funeral service was held for seven of the victims.
Distraught relatives hugged the coffins as robed Russian Orthodox priests intoned a requiem mass for the dead, who included the widow of veterans' leader Mikhail Likhodei.
It was Likhodei's own murder in a bomb blast on November 10 1994 that was being commemorated at the time of Sunday's explosion.
The bomb, equivalent to between two and five kg (4-10 lb) of high explosive, was placed under a table of food and drink and connected by wire to a detonator about 40 metres (yards) away.
Human remains were found up to 30 metres (yards) away from the blast.

Speaking after the church ceremony at the burial of Likhodei's widow Yelena, in a plot next to her husband's grave, Afghan veteran Andrei Chipurnoi said: "How are these people, these women and children, guilty? Why must they die?"

"These are certainly not the last victims and nobody can be sure that tomorrow there will not be another explosion," said Chipurnoi, whose Afghan War Invalids' Foundation was apparently the target of Sunday's blast.

Other speakers called for unity among the veterans' groups. Parliamentary deputy Sergei Baburin said those responsible for the explosion would be pursued relentlessly "however high their position and however great the capital at their disposal".
Thirteen people are still in hospital, 10 of them seriously injured, including a 10-year-old boy who has had an eye removed, Russian news agencies reported.
Criminal groupings are believed to have used the foundation, which benefited from tax and excise exemptions on imports and exports, to launder money and send it out of the country.
However the foundation lost this right, estimated to have cost the treasury billions of dollars in lost taxes, in 1995 and the real motives of the explosion remain shrouded in mystery.
Some newspapers have speculated about a link much higher up the ladder of power than feuding veteran groups.

Investigators are examining camera footage of the memorial service taken by two Russian journalists killed in the blast. Interfax news agency said a photo-fit had been compiled of a "suspicious-looking man" seen at the cemetery before the blast.
"We will take all necessary measures to uncover this crime," said Deputy Interior Minister Vladimir Kolesnikov.

His ministry is also currently investigating the gunning down of a U.S. businessman, Paul Tatum, on November 3 outside a Moscow hotel whose ownership he was disputing. Tatum's funeral was also due to take place on Thursday.
Kolesnikov dismissed media claims that the government was losing the battle against organised crime, saying some 1.6 million crimes had been solved in the past 10 months, including 20,000 murders.
